h1: Overhead cabinets up to the ceiling
lead: An overhead cabinet uses the space between the wardrobe and the ceiling for duvets and suitcases. You add it in our 3D designer and see straight away what it adds to the price.
body:
Above most wardrobes there is a strip of wall left up to the ceiling. If anything is up there, it is often a box you have to stand on a chair to reach, and a layer of dust. An overhead cabinet is a separate cabinet with its own doors that stands on top of the wardrobe, so the space becomes closed storage.

You add the overhead cabinet in [our 3D designer](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab) while you build the wardrobes. Here you can read what it is used for, and what it costs in the three heights.

## What an overhead cabinet is used for

The overhead cabinet is for the things you will not need tomorrow. The duvets for the guest bed and the suitcases take up a lot of space and are rarely needed, so they can sit behind a door you have to reach up for. The same goes for things you only take out once a year, such as the Christmas decorations.

When those things are in the overhead cabinet, the hat shelf in the wardrobe below is free for what you use every day. The overhead cabinet has the same width and depth as the wardrobe it stands on.

## The overhead cabinet finishes the wall up to the ceiling

A wall of wardrobes that stops some way below the ceiling looks like a piece of furniture placed against the wall. If it goes all the way up, it looks as if it belongs to the room. The wardrobes can be up to 240 cm high, and if the ceiling is higher, the overhead cabinet takes the wall the last bit of the way.

The overhead cabinet is built in the same material as the wardrobes, and the doors have the same finish as the doors below, so the wall reads as one. The designer shows the wardrobes free-standing, but we draw them to fit the room. If the wall is to go all the way up to the ceiling, write it in the message when you send it.

If there is only a little space above the wardrobe, it can pay to make the wardrobe itself taller. That is cheaper than an overhead cabinet, because the overhead cabinet is a complete cabinet of its own with its own sides and doors. On the other hand, in the overhead cabinet the duvets sit behind their own door and not on the hat shelf above the clothes.

## Three heights, and what the overhead cabinet costs

The overhead cabinet comes in 30, 40 and 50 cm. Which height you choose depends mostly on how much wall is left up to the ceiling. The designer shows how high the wardrobe and overhead cabinet are together, so you can compare it with your own measurement from floor to ceiling. You can give each wardrobe its own overhead cabinet or put the same one on the whole wall.

The table shows the same wardrobe in oak veneer, 60 cm wide, 210 cm high and 60 cm deep, with a hat shelf and hanging rail. The prices are incl. VAT and without delivery, for a flat-packed wardrobe.

| Wardrobe in oak veneer | Price for the wardrobe | Extra |
|---|---|---|
| Without overhead cabinet | [DKK 11,250](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab&t=e30) | Base price |
| Overhead cabinet of 30 cm | [DKK 13,850](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab&t=eyJ0b3AiOjMwfQ) | +DKK 2,600 |
| Overhead cabinet of 40 cm | [DKK 14,225](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab&t=eyJ0b3AiOjQwfQ) | +DKK 2,975 |
| Overhead cabinet of 50 cm | [DKK 15,050](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab&t=eyJ0b3AiOjUwfQ) | +DKK 3,800 |
| Wardrobe 240 cm high, without overhead cabinet | [DKK 12,325](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab&t=eyJoIjoyNDB9) | +DKK 1,075 |

More sizes and materials are in the [price guide](/hvad-koster-et-garderobeskab).

## Overhead cabinet above a bench

One of the cabinets in the wall can be a low [bench](/opbevaringsbaenk) with drawers under the seat and a cushion on top. Above the bench there can be an overhead cabinet at the top, level with the rest of the wall, or the space can be left open for jackets.

The frame can be added. Then the overhead cabinet above the bench gets a cover panel on top and sides down to the floor at the ends that do not stand against a cabinet, and the bench stands in an opening in the wall. Without the frame, the overhead cabinet hangs freely above the bench.

## From drawing to wardrobe

When you send the wall of wardrobes from the designer, it is an enquiry, not an order. We send a quote and a drawing with the final measurements, and you approve the drawing before we build the wardrobes in our own production. It takes 3 to 6 weeks from order to delivery, and we deliver throughout Denmark.

The wardrobes and overhead cabinets are supplied flat-packed with assembly instructions, and that is how the prices above are calculated. If you want them delivered assembled, there is an extra charge for freight, and if we are to carry the wardrobes in and install them, they must be assembled. You choose delivery for the whole order in the designer's basket, and the price is shown there before you send. If you are unsure of the height to the ceiling, you can add a site survey.

If the designer cannot do what you want, [send us a sketch](/kontakt?emne=Overskabe) with measurements. Read more about [made-to-measure wardrobes](/garderobeskab), or see [examples from the designer](/design-det-selv).

h1: Compact laminate cabinets for bathrooms and wet rooms
lead: A cabinet under a basin gets wet where ordinary cabinets are weakest: at the bottom and at the holes for the pipes. Compact laminate cabinets have no wood core, so there is nothing that can swell.
body:
Compact laminate cabinets are for places where a cabinet gets wet or is washed down every day: under the basin in a bathroom, in a baby changing room, a cleaning room or a changing room. An ordinary cabinet is built from chipboard or MDF with a melamine or laminate surface. The surface takes water, but the edges and the holes for hinges and pipes do not. Once water has got in there, the board swells, and the cabinet has to be replaced.

## The water comes from below and at the pipes

Under a basin, water pipes and the drain run through the cabinet, and a drip from the trap or a loose hose ends up at the bottom. In a bathroom, the floor is washed, and the water stands against the plinth. Those are the places where a chipboard cabinet is damaged first, and the damage is often only seen once the bottom has lifted.

If the whole cabinet is built in [compact laminate](/kompaktlaminat), the bottom, sides and back are the same dense material as the door. There is no edge banding that can come loose, and a hole for a pipe does not open into a core that can soak up water. The cabinet can stand on a plinth or on adjustable legs, so you can clean under it.

A tall cabinet that stands a little away from the water can be built with the visible surfaces in compact laminate. That is how we are building the tall cabinets in the wet rooms at Vinge Daycare Centre, with visible surfaces in the same compact laminate as the toilet cubicles. Read more about [toilet cubicles](/toiletbaase).

## Many identical cabinets for a housing project

In the renovation of the housing blocks at Bølholmen in Stenløse, we have delivered 230 identical under-basin cabinets in compact laminate for 220 homes for the main contractor Enemærke & Petersen. The cabinets are in use today.

In a housing project, the same cabinet is repeated home after home, and a mistake in the drawing is repeated just as many times. For series with many identical units, we are therefore happy to build a sample piece first, so the joints, the door and the hinges are tested before the rest goes into production. We agree delivery with the main contractor, so the cabinets arrive in stages as the homes are ready for them. See [furniture for housing projects](/inventar-til-boligbyggeri).

## Compact laminate where the cabinet stands wet

Compact laminate is an expensive material. A cabinet in compact laminate costs almost twice as much as the same cabinet in pine plywood, so the money is well spent under the basin and in the wet room, but rarely in an entrance hall or a dry storeroom. If the project is not yet out to tender, we are happy to give an estimate and point out which cabinets stand wet enough to be worth building in compact laminate. If the cabinets stay dry, see [plywood cabinets](/skabe-i-krydsfiner).

We measure on site where pipes and installations decide the dimensions, and draw the cabinets in 3D from that. You approve the workshop drawings before we go into production. Shelves, doors and locks are adapted to the use, and if the cabinets are for a changing room, you can read more about [changing room cabinets](/omklaedningsskabe).

Below the text are examples from our 3D designer, where you can put together wardrobes and lockers in compact laminate and see the price as you choose.

faq.a: It depends on the scope, and on when the building needs the cabinets. Include the installation date when you ask for a price, and we plan production around it from the start. If the cabinets are delivered in stages, we plan production around the stages.

h1: Compact laminate for toilet cubicles, wash counters and wet rooms
lead: Compact laminate is laminate all the way through and does not soak up water. We use it where water hits the furniture, and choose wood where the room is dry enough for it.
body:
In a toilet room or a changing room, the furniture is washed down every day, and the water runs down the edges and stands on the floor. A piece of furniture made of chipboard or MDF with a laminate surface lasts until the water finds an edge or a screw hole. Then the board soaks it up and swells, and that damage cannot be repaired. Compact laminate has no wood core. The board is laminate all the way through, so there is nowhere for the water to get in.

## Compact laminate where water hits, wood in the rest of the room

A wet room is not equally wet everywhere. At the basin and under the showers, the surfaces get wet several times a day. A couple of metres away, it is mostly the moisture in the air that the furniture has to withstand. That is why we use compact laminate where water hits, and wood where it is only damp. It matters for the price, because a cabinet in compact laminate costs almost twice as much as the same cabinet in pine plywood.

In the changing rooms at Sundby Sports Park, which we are making for Ason A/S with WE Architecture as architect, the benches are solid pine and the wash counters are compact laminate. Each of the nine wash counters has a basin and a tap and stands on a pine frame, and the tops come in five colours that set the rooms apart. Read more about [changing room furniture and wash counters](/omklaedning).

At a swimming pool, the air is damp all day, also far from the showers. Here it makes sense to build most of the changing room in compact laminate. See [furniture for swimming pools](/inventar-til-svoemmehaller).

## The board supports itself

Compact laminate is dense and stiff enough to stand alone. A partition in a toilet cubicle can stand on legs and be held by brackets in the wall without a frame around it, and a wash counter can carry the basin without another board underneath. The furniture is therefore built from fewer parts, and there are fewer joints where dirt and water can collect.

The edge does not need closing with edge banding. It is sanded and left visible, and the core shows as a thin stripe along the edge, usually black. On a light board, the black core outlines the shape of the furniture. If the architect wants a calmer look, there are boards with a white or coloured core.

## What we build in compact laminate

For Vinge Daycare Centre, working for Kanneworff & Viuff, we are making toilet cubicles and privacy screens at the changing tables in compact laminate, and the tall cabinets in the wet rooms have visible surfaces in the same material. The cubicles stand on adjustable legs, so the floor can be washed under them. Read more about [toilet cubicles](/toiletbaase).

In the renovation of the housing blocks at Bølholmen in Stenløse, we have delivered 230 identical under-basin cabinets in compact laminate for 220 homes for Enemærke & Petersen. The cabinets are in use today. See [compact laminate cabinets](/kompaktlaminat-skabe).

## From drawing to installation

A hole for a basin or a tap cannot be moved once the board has been cut. That is why we draw the furniture in 3D from the architect's drawings and measure on site where a dimension depends on the building. The workshop drawings, which you approve, and the parts list that production builds from come from the same model, so the holes sit where the basin is to go.

The difference between compact laminate and laminate on a core board, and why it shows in the edge, is explained in the guide [compact laminate vs laminate](/kompaktlaminat-eller-laminat).

faq.q: Can compact laminate stand where there is water on the floor?
faq.a: Yes. The board has no wood core and does not soak up water, not even at edges and drilled holes. It can be washed down every day and stand in a room where the floor is wet.

faq.q: Why not build the whole changing room in compact laminate?
faq.a: You can, and at a swimming pool it often makes sense. But compact laminate is more expensive than plywood, and the surface cannot be sanded and re-oiled when it gets scratched. Where it is only damp, oiled wood is often the better choice, and in an estimate we are happy to show where the line goes.

faq.q: What colours does compact laminate come in?
faq.a: The boards come in many solid colours and with decors. For Sundby Sports Park the wash counters are in five colours that set the changing rooms apart. We agree colour and core with the architect before the boards are ordered.

faq.q: Can you supply documentation for Nordic Swan Ecolabel buildings?
faq.a: Yes. If the building is to carry the Nordic Swan Ecolabel, we collect the documentation for the boards for the building's material log. If the tender requires FSC- or PEFC-certified material, the quote states which boards can be supplied with certification.

faq.q: What should we send to get a price?
faq.a: The drawings, the full joinery specification and the bill of quantities, and ideally the schedule with the installation date. Also tell us whether the architect has chosen the colours. Send it to tilbud@neminventar.dk, and you get a price per item, with reservations and questions gathered in the quote.

h1: Fixed furniture as a subcontract for main contractors
lead: Fixed furniture is many small items that come late in the build and have to fit in between the other trades. We take them as one subcontract, priced on your tender documents and produced to your installation date.
body:
We deliver fixed furniture as a subcontract for the main contractor, or as a trade contract directly to the client when the furniture is tendered separately. The furniture is many small items spread over many rooms, and it comes in late, when floors and walls are finished and handover is close. These are items that need to be under control already in the quote, and we bring them together, so you have one contact for all the furniture from quote to installation.

## A quote you can put next to the others

We price each item on the bill of quantities as it stands. If we find differences between the drawings and the list, we write them as reservations instead of correcting the list, so you can compare our price with the others you receive. Requirements for surfaces and fittings are often in the general sections of the joinery specification, so we go through those too before we price.

What we have not priced is also stated in the quote. This is where an item would otherwise fall between two contracts. When it is written down, you can place it with someone else before the contract is signed, instead of finding the gap on site.

## Production is planned to the installation date

We need the installation date when you ask for a price. The furniture is produced in our own production, and we plan production around that date from the start, so the furniture is finished before we go in. If it is to be delivered in phases, we plan production around the phases and agree them with you, e.g. one wing or one floor at a time.

The site decides how the furniture goes in. At Mørkhøj School we are delivering for Ason A/S in phases following the site schedule, and the first phase has been handed over and is in use. At Vinge Daycare Centre, where Kanneworff & Viuff is the contractor, everything is installed together in one go.

## The drawings come early

The workshop drawings have to be approved by the architect and contractor before we produce, so the approval is a date in your schedule. We draw the furniture in 3D from the architect's drawings, and the same model gives both the drawings for approval and the parts list that production builds from. If a dimension changes after approval, we correct it in the model, and the drawings and parts list are updated together.

Where a dimension depends on the building, we carry out a site survey. For series with many identical elements, we are happy to build a sample piece, which is approved before the rest goes into production, so a mistake is found on one element and not on the whole series. Read more about [workshop drawings and the 3D model](/vaerkstedstegninger-og-3d-model).

## Installation and responsibility in one place

We also install the furniture, so the responsibility for it fitting sits in the same place as the drawings and production. At Sundby Sports Park, also for Ason A/S, we handle the whole process from site survey to installation of the changing rooms in two halls.

For Enemærke & Petersen, we delivered 230 identical under-basin cabinets in compact laminate for 220 homes in the renovation of the housing blocks at Bølholmen in Stenløse. You can read about series under [furniture for housing](/inventar-til-boligbyggeri), and about buildings that stay in use in the meantime under [furniture in renovation projects](/inventar-ved-renovering).

If the building is to carry the Nordic Swan Ecolabel, we supply the material documentation for the building's materials log, see [furniture for Nordic Swan Ecolabel buildings](/inventar-til-svanemaerket-byggeri). What to send to get a price is explained under [requesting a quote for fixed furniture](/forespoergsel-paa-fast-inventar).

faq.a: The drawings, the full joinery specification with the general sections, the bill of quantities and the schedule with the installation date. Send it to tilbud@neminventar.dk. Reservations and questions are collected in the quote.

faq.q: Can you deliver in phases?
faq.a: Yes. We plan production around the phases we agree with you, so the furniture for each phase is finished before we go in. If everything has to be installed at once, we do that.

faq.q: Do you also handle installation?
faq.a: Yes. We install the furniture, so the responsibility for product and installation sits in one place.

faq.a: It depends on the scope and on when the site is ready. Include the installation date when you ask for a price, and we will plan production around it from the start.

h1: Acoustic panels to measure in textile or plywood
lead: We make acoustic panels to measure in textile and in perforated plywood. The choice depends mostly on the room and on what the wall is exposed to, and here you can read how we choose.
body:
Acoustic panels reduce reverberation, so it becomes easier to speak and hear in a room with hard surfaces. We make acoustic panels to measure in two versions: upholstered panels in textile and panels in perforated plywood with round holes. Both absorb sound, but they do not take the same wear, so it is usually the wear in the room that decides the choice.

How many panels are needed, and where they go, is set out in the acoustician's report on the room's acoustic treatment, and we draw the panels to the report and the room's dimensions. How long the reverberation time may be in a classroom or a daycare centre, and how much the panels help in your own room, is covered under [reverberation time](/efterklangstid). The ceiling is one of the room's largest surfaces and matters a lot for the reverberation time, so tell us how the ceiling is built when you send the drawings.

## Textile where the wall is mostly looked at

An upholstered acoustic panel is an acoustic board on a rigid backing board, covered with acoustic textile. The whole soft surface takes in the sound, so the panel absorbs wherever the sound hits it. It suits classrooms and meeting rooms, where the hard sound has to go without the wall drawing attention to itself.

The fabric can be touched, but it is a soft surface, and it gets worn and dirty first where hands and bags hit it every day. That is why the cover can be replaced while the rest of the panel stays on the wall, and the panels can be placed high enough on the wall for most of the wear to pass them by.

The panels are sewn and built to measure with no minimum quantity, so they can fit between boards and above cabinets. The fabric is coloured, and different shades can be mixed on the same wall, so it comes alive without dominating the room.

At Mørkhøj School we are delivering approx. 300 m² of textile acoustic panels for classrooms and common areas as part of the fixed furniture for the main contractor Ason A/S. How the panels sit together with the boards in the classroom is shown under [acoustics and glass boards](/akustik-og-glastavler).

## Perforated plywood where the wall also gets hit

An acoustic panel in perforated plywood is a wooden panel with round holes and a cavity with mineral wool behind. The sound passes through the holes and is absorbed in the mineral wool. The surface you see and touch is wood, so it can take being hit by a ball or a chair, and it can be made in the same wood and the same oil as the cabinets and benches in the room. That makes plywood suitable for corridors and [sports halls](/inventar-til-idraetshaller), where the wall gets hit every day.

Surfaces that do not need to absorb sound are made from the same panel without holes, so the wall looks the same all the way along. The holes can also form a motif, e.g. waves, or leave a logo smooth in the wood. The panel is birch or pine plywood, clear-oiled or in one of our colours, and it is also available as fire-retardant plywood.

How much the panel absorbs depends on how much of it is holes and on the cavity behind it. With our standard hole pattern and 4 cm of mineral wool behind the panel, our calculation gives αw approx. 0.70, absorption class C, and with 3 cm of mineral wool αw approx. 0.65. The figures are calculated from publicly available measurements of perforated wood panels and are not measured on our own panel. How we calculated is explained under [calculating sound absorption](/beregning-af-lydabsorption), and the absorption in each octave band under [acoustic walls in perforated plywood](/akustikvaegge-perforeret-krydsfiner).

In our [3D designer for acoustic panels](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=akustik) you can draw a field in perforated plywood with your dimensions and hole pattern and see the price and an estimate of the absorption as you go.

## Textile in the classroom, plywood in the corridor

In a school there is rarely one answer for the whole building. In the classroom, where the wall is mostly looked at, textile does the job, and the cover can be replaced when it is worn. In the corridor outside, where bags and balls hit the wall, plywood takes the wear, and it can be in the same wood as the cloakroom. We are happy to price both, so you can see what the choice means in your project.

## What we need to give you a price

Send drawings with wall dimensions and the ceiling build-up, the joinery specification and, if you have it, the acoustician's report to tilbud@neminventar.dk. If the project is out to tender, we price each item in the bill of quantities, and if it is earlier in the design stage, we are happy to give an estimate from the material available. The panels are drawn in 3D together with the rest of the furniture, and you approve the workshop drawings before we produce. Read more about [workshop drawings and 3D model](/vaerkstedstegninger-og-3d-model).

faq.q: Should we choose acoustic panels in textile or in plywood?
faq.a: It depends on what the wall is exposed to. Textile suits places where the wall is mostly looked at and touched, e.g. in a classroom or a meeting room, and the cover can be replaced when it is worn. Perforated plywood suits places where balls and chairs hit the wall, or where the acoustics should be in the same wood as the rest of the furniture. In a school it often makes sense to use textile in the classrooms and plywood in the corridors.

faq.q: How much does an acoustic panel in perforated plywood absorb?
faq.a: With our standard hole pattern and 4 cm of mineral wool behind the panel, our calculation gives αw approx. 0.70, absorption class C, and with 3 cm of mineral wool αw approx. 0.65. The figures are calculated from publicly available measurements of perforated wood panels and not measured on our own panel. See [calculating sound absorption](/beregning-af-lydabsorption). The acoustician's calculation of the room sets the project's values.

faq.q: Can the cover on a textile acoustic panel be replaced?
faq.a: Yes. If the fabric gets worn, or the wall needs a different colour, the cover is replaced while the rest of the panel stays on the wall.

faq.q: Can you supply acoustic panels in fire-retardant plywood?
faq.a: Yes. The panels in perforated plywood can be made in fire-retardant plywood. Mention it in your enquiry, and we will allow for it.

faq.q: Can the acoustic panels have the same colour as the rest of the furniture?
faq.a: The plywood panels are clear-oiled or oiled in one of our colours, so they can be the same colour as the cabinets and benches in the room. The textile panels are covered with coloured fabric, and shades can be mixed on the same wall.

faq.q: What should we send to get a price on acoustic panels?
faq.a: Drawings with wall dimensions and the ceiling build-up, the joinery specification and, if you have it, the acoustician's report. Send it to tilbud@neminventar.dk. If the project is out to tender, we price each item, and if it is earlier, we are happy to give an estimate from the material available.

faq.q: How much do acoustic panels help?
faq.a: It depends on how much the room absorbs already. The reverberation time follows Sabine's formula, T = 0.161 · V / A, so when the room's total absorption doubles, the reverberation time halves. In a classroom of 9 by 7 metres and 3 metres high with a hard ceiling and no other acoustic treatment, the reverberation time is 3.4 seconds at 1000 Hz, and five panels in perforated plywood, 7.2 m² in total, take it down to 2.0 seconds. The panels absorb least in the bass, so in a hard room more than one wall of panels is needed to reach the requirement of 0.6 seconds. If the room is already close to the requirement, a field of panels on one wall can be enough. Under [reverberation time](/efterklangstid) you can calculate your own room.

faq.q: How long may the reverberation time be in schools and daycare centres?
faq.a: Under the guidance to the Danish Building Regulations, at most 0.6 seconds in classrooms and 0.4 seconds in common rooms for group work and in playrooms in daycare centres, in every octave band from 125 to 4000 Hz. At 125 Hz the time may be 20 % longer, and the limit values apply in furnished rooms. The requirements are in the guidance for educational buildings, table 3.4, and in the guidance for daycare buildings, table 4.4. The acoustician's calculation of the room decides how many panels are needed.

faq.q: Can you supply the acoustic panels together with the rest of the school's furniture?
faq.a: Yes. The panels are drawn in 3D together with the rest of the fixed furniture, and you approve the workshop drawings before we produce. At Mørkhøj School we are delivering approx. 300 m² of textile acoustic panels for classrooms and common areas as part of the fixed furniture for the main contractor Ason A/S.

h1: Fixed furniture for architects and consultants
lead: You have drawn the furniture, and you should recognise it when it stands in the room. We draw it in 3D from your drawings and specification, and you approve the workshop drawings before we start production.
body:
We build fixed furniture from the architect's drawings and joinery specification, most often as a subcontract for the main contractor. For you as architects and consultants, what matters most is that what gets built is what you drew, right down to the edge and the colour. That has to be settled before the first board is cut, not when the furniture is standing in the room.

## The details are settled in the 3D model

Once the order is in place, we draw each element in 3D from your drawings and carry out a site survey where a dimension depends on the building. The model is where it shows whether a joint or a corner can be built as drawn. If it cannot, we show another solution on the workshop drawing, and you approve it before we start production.

The workshop drawings you approve and the parts list that production builds from come from the same model. If you change a dimension or a detail after the drawings have been sent, we change it in the model, and the drawings and parts list are updated together. That way it is your latest approved drawing that gets built. Read more about [workshop drawings and the 3D model](/vaerkstedstegninger-og-3d-model).

At Mørkhøj School, every room was drawn in 3D and approved before it went into production, and colours and materials were settled with Rønnow Arkitekter and the client. The wood is oiled in two colours mixed for us, and the surface can be refreshed in patches where it wears.

## The material is part of the look

Plywood is thin layers of wood laid crosswise, and the layers show as stripes on the edge. If you leave the edge visible, the furniture shows how the board is built up, and that is a detail you can draw on purpose on a shelf or a wall cladding. If the plywood is oiled in a colour, the grain still shows through the colour.

Compact laminate is laminate all the way through, so the edge can be left without edge banding. The core often has a different colour from the surface and shows as a thin line along the edge, so here too the edge is part of the drawing. The difference between compact laminate and ordinary laminate is explained in [compact laminate vs laminate](/kompaktlaminat-eller-laminat).

For a sports hall, we made 43 shoe racks in birch plywood with a bench on top and clad the columns and the continuous beam in the same plywood, so furniture and building belong together. At Sundby Sports Park, where WE Architecture is the architect, wash counters in compact laminate in five colours divide up the changing rooms.

If a wall has to absorb sound and be a wooden surface at the same time, we make acoustic panels in plywood with holes and acoustic felt behind. The hole pattern is drawn to the room's dimensions and the acoustic engineer's requirements, so it becomes part of the look of the wall. See [acoustic walls in perforated plywood](/akustikvaegge-perforeret-krydsfiner).

## The specification is what we price

We price and build from your specification, including the general sections, where the requirements for surfaces and fittings are often found. Our starting point is oil on plywood, but if the specification calls for lacquer, lacquer is what we price and deliver. If we find differences between the drawings and the bill of quantities, we write them as reservations instead of correcting the list ourselves, so the choice stays with you.

If you are still at the design stage, we are happy to give an estimate for the furniture based on the material available and point out where a choice of material or a detail moves the price. This is where a choice can still be changed without it becoming a change on the building site.

## A sample piece before the series

For series with many identical elements, we are happy to build a sample piece first. Then you see the colour and the edge on a real piece and not only on a drawing, and the joints and fittings have been tested before we produce the rest in our own production.

If the building is to carry the Nordic Swan Ecolabel or be DGNB-certified, the documentation has to cover the materials in your specification. We choose materials that can be approved and collect the documentation for the building's materials log. Read more about [furniture for Nordic Swan Ecolabel buildings](/inventar-til-svanemaerket-byggeri) and about how we work for [the main contractor](/inventar-til-hovedentreprenoerer).

faq.q: What do we get to approve before production?
faq.a: Workshop drawings with dimensions and details for each element, taken from the 3D model. The parts list for production comes from the same model, so what you approve is what we build. For series with many identical elements, we are happy to build a sample piece first.

faq.q: Do you build to our specification, or do you suggest other materials?
faq.a: We price and build to the specification. Our starting point is oil on plywood, but if the specification calls for lacquer, lacquer is what you get. If we see a choice that moves the price a lot, we say so, and then you decide.

faq.q: Can you give an estimate while we are designing?
faq.a: Yes. Send the material you have, and we will give an estimate for the furniture and point out where a choice of material or a detail moves the price. It is easiest to change before the specification is locked.

faq.q: Can the colours be matched to the rest of the building?
faq.a: Yes. Plywood can be oiled in a colour, and laminate comes in many colours. We agree the colours with you before we start production. At Mørkhøj School, the wood is oiled in two colours mixed for us.

faq.q: Can you make acoustic panels in wood?
faq.a: Yes, in plywood with holes and acoustic felt behind. The hole pattern is drawn to the room's dimensions and the acoustic engineer's requirements.

faq.q: Do you supply documentation for Nordic Swan Ecolabel buildings?
faq.a: Yes. We supply material documentation for the building's materials log and a timber account showing the share of certified wood, and the same documentation can be used in a DGNB building. If the specification requires FSC or PEFC wood, the quote states which boards can be supplied with certification.

h1: Acoustic walls in perforated plywood
lead: Here you can see how much a wall in perforated plywood absorbs in each octave band, why a deeper cavity absorbs more bass, and what an acoustic wall does to the reverberation time in a classroom. The figures are calculated and based on publicly available measurements of perforated panels, not on our own.
body:
Perforated plywood is a wooden panel with a pattern of holes. Behind the panel is a cavity with mineral wool. Between the panel and the mineral wool there is an acoustic fleece. The sound passes through the holes, and in the mineral wool it turns into heat, so the reverberation in the room drops. The surface you see and touch is wood. It stands up to hands, balls and chairs, and it can be made in the same wood and the same oil as the cabinets and benches in the room.

With holes of 0.8 cm at 1.6 cm centre to centre and 4 cm of mineral wool behind, an acoustic wall in 1.2 cm plywood has, by our calculation, a weighted sound absorption coefficient αw of approx. 0.70. That is absorption class C under EN ISO 11654. All figures on this page are calculated. They are not based on measurements of our own panel, but on a model we have calibrated against publicly available measurements from manufacturers' data sheets and a diploma thesis. How the calculation is made is explained under [calculating sound absorption](/beregning-af-lydabsorption).

## The deeper the cavity, the more bass it absorbs

The air in each hole is a small mass, and the air in the cavity behind the panel acts as a spring. Together they vibrate most easily at one frequency, and that is where the wall absorbs most. The mineral wool slows the air down and spreads the absorption over several octaves. Without mineral wool the absorption is narrow, and it depends on how airtight the build-up is at joints and battens. The model is only calibrated against build-ups with mineral wool or felt behind the panel, so we only calculate build-ups with mineral wool.

A deeper cavity is a softer spring, so the wall absorbs most at a lower frequency. That is why a deeper cavity absorbs more bass. The table shows the same hole pattern with the two build-ups we calculate with behind the panel. The figures are the practical sound absorption coefficient αp in each octave band, where 0 means the surface reflects all the sound and 1 means it absorbs all of it.

| Octave band | 3 cm cavity filled with mineral wool | 4 cm cavity filled with mineral wool |
|---|---|---|
| 125 Hz | 0.15 | 0.25 |
| 250 Hz | 0.40 | 0.55 |
| 500 Hz | 0.80 | 0.90 |
| 1000 Hz | 0.95 | 0.90 |
| 2000 Hz | 0.70 | 0.70 |
| 4000 Hz | 0.55 | 0.55 |
| αw and class | 0.65 (C) | 0.70 (C) |

From a 3 cm to a 4 cm cavity, the absorption at 125 Hz rises from 0.15 to 0.25 and at 250 Hz from 0.40 to 0.55, and αw rises from 0.65 to 0.70. Under EN ISO 11654, αw is calculated only from 250 to 4000 Hz. The bass at 125 Hz does not count at all, and it is 2000 and 4000 Hz that hold the figure down with 4 cm, and 250 and 4000 Hz with 3 cm. When a reverberation time requirement applies all the way down to 125 Hz, it is the figures per octave that must be compared.

## The open area shifts the absorption

The open area is the part of the panel that is holes. The table shows the four hole patterns in our acoustic designer with 4 cm of mineral wool behind. The open area is calculated over the whole panel, for panels that are 60 cm wide and 240 cm high with a 2 cm border without holes. In the Dense pattern the holes sit in staggered rows, so the distance to all neighbours is the same.

| Hole pattern | Sparse | Standard | Dense | Fine |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hole diameter | 0.8 cm | 0.8 cm | 0.6 cm | 0.4 cm |
| Centre to centre | 3.2 cm | 1.6 cm | 1.2 cm | 0.8 cm |
| Holes per m² in the perforated area | 977 | 3,906 | 8,019 | 15,625 |
| Open area | 4.7 % | 18.1 % | 20.7 % | 18.0 % |
| 125 Hz | 0.40 | 0.25 | 0.20 | 0.20 |
| 250 Hz | 0.70 | 0.55 | 0.50 | 0.50 |
| 500 Hz | 0.65 | 0.90 | 0.90 | 0.90 |
| 1000 Hz | 0.40 | 0.90 | 0.95 | 0.95 |
| 2000 Hz | 0.20 | 0.70 | 0.75 | 0.70 |
| 4000 Hz | 0.15 | 0.55 | 0.60 | 0.55 |
| αw and class | 0.25 (E) | 0.70 (C) | 0.75 (C) | 0.70 (C) |

Standard and Fine have almost the same open area and absorb almost the same, even though Fine has four times as many holes. Sparse has so little open area that the air in the holes becomes heavy. The absorption shifts down towards 250 Hz, and from 1000 Hz upwards the panel reflects most of the sound. Below 5 % open area the calculation is also least certain in the bass, because that is where the model performs worst against the measurements it has been tested on. With 3 cm of mineral wool behind, αw is 0.65 for Standard, Dense and Fine and 0.25 for Sparse.

## A classroom calculated against the BR18 requirement

The Danish Building Regulations, BR18, require the reverberation time in a classroom to be at most 0.6 seconds in every octave band from 125 to 4000 Hz. At 125 Hz it may be 20 % longer, which is 0.72 seconds. The requirement applies in furnished rooms and is stated in the guidance for educational buildings, table 3.4.

We have calculated the classroom the acoustic designer uses as its default. It is 9 metres long, 7 metres wide and 3 metres to the ceiling, 189 m³ in total. The walls are light plasterboard walls with windows and doors, the floor is linoleum on concrete, and wooden tables and chairs stand on a quarter of the floor. The acoustic wall is just over 3 metres wide and 2.4 metres high, 7.2 m² of panels in total with the Standard hole pattern and 4 cm of mineral wool behind, and it replaces a section of the plasterboard wall. The reverberation time is calculated with Sabine's formula for each octave band.

With a perforated plasterboard ceiling, the room is slightly above the requirement at 250 and 500 Hz. Here the acoustic wall brings the room below the requirement in five of six octave bands.

| Octave band | Without acoustic wall | With acoustic wall | BR18 requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| 125 Hz | 0.68 s | 0.67 s | 0.72 s |
| 250 Hz | 0.64 s | 0.60 s | 0.60 s |
| 500 Hz | 0.65 s | 0.57 s | 0.60 s |
| 1000 Hz | 0.47 s | 0.43 s | 0.60 s |
| 2000 Hz | 0.49 s | 0.46 s | 0.60 s |
| 4000 Hz | 0.55 s | 0.52 s | 0.60 s |

At 250 Hz the reverberation time lands at 0.601 seconds, a fraction above the requirement. By the calculation, at least 7.4 m² of panels are needed. That is 6 panels of 60 by 240 cm, 8.6 m² in total, and in the designer the nearest field is 7 panels, 10.1 m² in total. With 3 cm of mineral wool behind, approx. 11 m² is needed.

With a hard concrete ceiling it is a different matter. Without an acoustic wall the reverberation time is 1.8 seconds at 125 Hz and 3.4 seconds at 1000 Hz. The acoustic wall takes 1000 Hz down to 2.0 seconds, but 125 Hz only falls to 1.7. Even if the whole long wall of 27 m² were panels, the reverberation time would be 0.9 to 1.5 seconds. To reach 0.72 seconds at 125 Hz, the calculation says approx. 250 m² of panels would be needed, which is more than the room's four walls together. The panels absorb least in the bass, and it is 125 Hz that decides whether wall panels alone meet the requirement. In a room with a hard ceiling they rarely do. With a mineral wool acoustic ceiling the room meets the requirement without an acoustic wall, at 0.41 to 0.65 seconds.

This is a calculation, not a measurement in the room. The room's surfaces are calculated with typical table values, measured under ISO 354, and the room is calculated furnished and unoccupied, as the requirement is measured. Sabine's formula gives a slightly too long reverberation time in rooms with a lot of absorption, so the calculation errs on the safe side. The acoustician's calculation of the real room sets the project's values, and the reverberation time is measured in the finished room.

## Where the figures come from and how certain they are

The figures are calculated with a model for perforated panels, with Maa's model for the holes and Miki's for the mineral wool. None of the figures are measured on our own panel. The model is calibrated against 54 publicly available measurements of panels with through holes, 53 from five manufacturers' data sheets and one from a diploma thesis. On measurements the model had not seen, αw was on average 0.08 off, and four times out of five within 0.15. The uncertainty is greatest in the bass. The figures are therefore an estimate for a panel like ours. They are good for choosing a hole pattern and build-up, and the acoustician calculates the final values. The formulas, the measurements and the uncertainty in each octave band are under [calculating sound absorption](/beregning-af-lydabsorption).

## Calculate your own room in the designer

In the [acoustic designer](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=akustik) you draw the acoustic wall with width, height and hole pattern and see the estimated absorption straight away. In the Room step you choose what the room is used for and enter its dimensions and ceiling. The designer then shows the reverberation time in each octave band without and with the acoustic wall, the BR18 requirement, and how many m² of panels are needed. It is the same model and the same figures as on this page.

## The wood, and how to get a price

We work in pine and birch plywood, finished with oil or pigmented oil, so the acoustic wall matches the rest of the furniture. The panel can also be fire-retardant plywood. The holes are round and go straight through the panel. The panels can be installed with shadow gaps and designed so they can be taken down if there must be access to services behind. The same build-up can be used on cabinet fronts and installation walls.

We agree the hole pattern and build-up with the project's acoustician, so the wall fits the reverberation time requirement the room is designed for. [Send us drawings](/kontakt?emne=Akustikv%C3%A6g) with wall dimensions and, if you have it, the acoustician's report, and we will come back with a proposed build-up and a price. If you do not have a requirement yet, we price a typical build-up that the acoustician can calculate on. Textile panels are covered under [acoustic panels](/akustikpaneler).

faq.q: How much does perforated plywood absorb?
faq.a: With holes of 0.8 cm at 1.6 cm centre to centre and 4 cm of mineral wool behind, an acoustic wall in 1.2 cm plywood has, by our calculation, αw approx. 0.70, absorption class C. The absorption is 0.25 at 125 Hz, 0.90 at 500 Hz and 0.55 at 4000 Hz. With 3 cm of mineral wool behind, αw is 0.65, also absorption class C. The figures are calculated and based on 54 publicly available measurements of perforated panels, not on measurements of our own panel. On measurements the model had not seen, αw was on average 0.08 off. How the calculation is made is explained under [calculating sound absorption](/beregning-af-lydabsorption).

faq.q: What does BR18 require in a classroom?
faq.a: The reverberation time may be at most 0.6 seconds in every octave band from 125 to 4000 Hz. At 125 Hz it may be 20 % longer, which is 0.72 seconds. The requirement applies in furnished rooms and is stated in the BR18 guidance for educational buildings, table 3.4. Rooms for group work have a requirement of 0.4 seconds, and the same applies to playrooms in daycare centres.

faq.q: Can an acoustic wall alone bring a classroom below the requirement?
faq.a: It depends on the ceiling. In a classroom of 9 by 7 metres with a perforated plasterboard ceiling, 7 panels, 10.1 m² in total, make the room meet the requirement in all six octave bands. With a hard ceiling the reverberation time is 1.8 to 3.4 seconds without panels, and at 125 Hz the calculation says approx. 250 m² of panels would be needed. The panels absorb least in the bass, so in a room with a hard ceiling wall panels alone rarely meet the requirement.

faq.q: Why does a deeper cavity absorb more bass?
faq.a: The air in the holes is a small mass, and the air in the cavity behind the panel is a spring. A deeper cavity is a softer spring, so the wall absorbs most at a lower frequency. With the same hole pattern, the absorption at 125 Hz rises from 0.15 with a 3 cm cavity to 0.25 with 4 cm, and at 250 Hz from 0.40 to 0.55.

faq.q: What do αw and absorption class mean?
faq.a: αw is a single figure for how much a surface absorbs, calculated under EN ISO 11654 from the absorption from 250 to 4000 Hz. The absorption class follows from it: A from 0.90, B from 0.80, C from 0.60, D from 0.30 and E from 0.15. 125 Hz is not part of αw, so two build-ups with the same αw can absorb the bass very differently. Look at the figures per octave when the requirement applies from 125 Hz.

faq.q: Can we calculate the reverberation time for our own room?
faq.a: Yes. In the [acoustic designer](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=akustik), in the Room step, you choose what the room is used for and enter its dimensions and ceiling. You then see the reverberation time in each octave band without and with the acoustic wall, the BR18 requirement, and how many m² of panels are needed. It is an estimate, and the acoustician's calculation is the basis for the project.

faq.q: What do you need to give a price?
faq.a: Drawings with wall dimensions and, if you have it, the acoustician's requirement or report. If you do not have a requirement yet, we can price a typical build-up that the acoustician can calculate on.

h1: Cabinets in plywood and birch plywood
lead: A cabinet in a school is opened and closed by many hands every day. If the whole cabinet is plywood, it can take that wear, and it can be moved and repaired later. We choose the door to suit the room.
body:
Plywood cabinets can be built in two ways. Either only the doors are plywood, and the cabinet itself is melamine-faced chipboard. Or the whole cabinet is plywood, including the sides, the shelves and the back panel. We build both, and the choice depends on the use. A whole cabinet in pine or birch plywood takes a lot, so it makes sense in an institution, and many people also choose it for the look. It can be moved without breaking, and damage can be repaired instead of replacing the part.

## The cabinet behind the door takes more wear than you think

The cabinet itself, behind the doors, is called the carcass, and it is the carcass that carries the load. The hinges are screwed into the sides, and the bottom gets kicked when someone is looking for something in the cabinet. Plywood holds screws well, also close to the edge, so the hinges stay put, even when the door is slammed many times a day. Chipboard holds less well, especially a screw that has come loose and is put back in, and if water gets into an edge, it swells.

When the whole cabinet is plywood, it looks the same inside and out, and the edge can be left visible on shelves and sides without edge banding. If the cabinet stays closed in a dry room where the carcass is rarely seen, plywood doors on a melamine carcass can be enough. If you want to compare, we are happy to price both while the specification can still be changed.

## Pine or birch: you see it in the edge

Pine plywood has a warm tone and a lively grain with knots. Birch plywood is lighter and harder and has many thin layers, so the edge shows as fine, straight stripes. If the edge is to be visible around inset doors or on open shelves, birch gives the calmest edge. Birch costs more than pine, so on a project with many cabinets it is worth using birch where the edge is seen.

Birch plywood is not the same as birch veneer. Birch veneer is a thin layer of birch glued onto chipboard or MDF, so only the surface is birch, and the edge has to be covered with edge banding or a lipping. Birch plywood is layer upon layer of birch, so the edge shows the wood. The difference between the boards is explained in the guide [plywood, MDF or chipboard](/krydsfiner-mdf-eller-spaanplade).

## The door is what everyone sees

The door is the surface everyone sees and takes hold of. In oiled plywood, clear or coloured, the wood shows, and wear can be refreshed on site. A stained door gets colour while the grain can still be seen. How the colour is applied is explained in the [guide to finishing plywood](/skal-krydsfiner-grundes).

If the door has to be one solid colour and be wiped every day, it gets a high-pressure laminate face. The plywood edge is still visible around the laminate, so the door belongs with the rest of the cabinet. If the door sits flush inside the cabinet, the layered edge forms a frame around it.

In [cloakrooms](/garderober), the doors can be perforated to let air reach the clothes. They can open with a push, so there is no handle that can break off or catch on clothes.

## Cabinets from our projects

For Hou School we are building cloakroom cabinets with lockable doors and an upholstered seating niche, where both the carcass and the doors are pine plywood, finished with oil. For the club meeting room at Sundby Sports Park we are making a [kitchenette](/tekoekkener-og-koekkenoer) in pine plywood with a linoleum worktop and space for a dishwasher and a freezer.

The classrooms at Mørkhøj School have tall cabinets in blue oiled plywood, in the school's colours. Each room was drawn in 3D and approved before the cabinets went into production. More plywood projects are shown under [plywood furniture](/krydsfiner-inventar).

## Drawn to fit the room

The cabinets are drawn in 3D from the architect's drawings, and where a dimension depends on the building, we measure on site. The workshop drawings, which you approve, and the parts list that our own production builds from come from the same model. For series of identical cabinets, we are happy to build a sample piece first, so hinges and lock are tested.

If the cabinets are to stand where water hits directly, see [compact laminate cabinets](/kompaktlaminat-skabe). The examples below were built in our 3D designer, where you can try cabinets in pine or birch plywood with coloured oil or laminate doors.

faq.q: Is the whole cabinet plywood, or only the doors?
faq.a: We build both, and it depends on the use. If the cabinet has to take a lot or be moved, a whole cabinet in plywood is the strongest choice, including carcass, shelves and back panel. If the cabinet stays closed in a dry room, plywood doors on a melamine carcass can be enough, and if you want to compare, we are happy to price both before the specification is fixed.

faq.q: What is the difference between birch plywood and birch veneer?
faq.a: Birch veneer is a thin layer of birch on another board, usually chipboard or MDF, so only the surface is birch, and the edge has to be covered. Birch plywood is layer upon layer of birch, so the edge shows the layers and can be left visible.

faq.q: Should we choose pine or birch?
faq.a: Birch is lighter and harder and has the finest edge, so it suits places where the edge is visible. Pine has a warmer tone, has knots and costs less.

faq.q: Can the doors have a different colour from the wood?
faq.a: Yes. Coloured oil or stain adds colour while the grain can still be seen. If the door has to be one solid colour, it gets a high-pressure laminate face, and the plywood edge stays visible around it. We agree the colour with the architect.

faq.q: Can plywood cabinets stand in damp rooms?
faq.a: In a cloakroom with wet jackets, yes. Where water hits directly, such as at a sink or in a bathroom, we build the cabinets in compact laminate, which does not soak up water.

faq.q: What does a plywood cabinet cost?
faq.a: The material moves the price most. Send the drawings, the full joinery specification and the bill of quantities to tilbud@neminventar.dk, and you get a price per item. If the project is not yet out to tender, we are happy to give an estimate and point out where a choice moves the price.

h1: Plywood furniture for schools and institutions
lead: Plywood is our starting point for fixed furniture that many people use every day. Here you can read why the board stands up to daily use in an institution, and where we swap it for something else.
body:
Plywood furniture is our starting point when we build fixed furniture for schools and daycare centres. The [cloakroom](/garderober) and the shoe rack in the corridor are used by many people every day and cleaned just as often, and that is where furniture in plywood does its job. Where water hits directly, we switch to compact laminate.

## The board holds up where the wear happens

Plywood is thin layers of wood glued together with the grain running crosswise. The layers hold each other, so the board moves far less than solid wood and is strong for its weight. For the furniture, this means that the screws in a hinge or a coat hook stay put, even when the door is slammed and the hook is pulled on many times a day.

The wear happens in the same places: at the bottom, where boots and bags hit, and on the edges, where people take hold. A knock to plywood leaves a dent or a splinter in the outer layer, but the board is wood all the way through, so no other material shows under the surface. The edge shows the layers as stripes and can be left visible without edge banding that can come loose.

## Oil, so wear can be repaired where it happens

Our starting point is oil. The oil goes into the wood instead of laying a film on top, and when a corner is worn after a few years, it can be refreshed with new oil on the spot, without sanding down the whole piece of furniture. That is why we oil the cloakrooms for Hou School rather than lacquer them, and the 43 shoe racks we have delivered to a sports hall are oiled for the same reason: the surface can be maintained on site.

Lacquer gives a closed surface, but a scratch in the lacquer cannot be repaired in patches in the same way. If the joinery specification calls for lacquer, lacquer is what we price and deliver. We also make lacquered plywood furniture, e.g. the locker cabinets with 150 lockable compartments for the changing rooms at Sundby Sports Park. How oil and lacquer are applied, and when plywood needs priming, is explained in the [guide to finishing plywood](/skal-krydsfiner-grundes).

## The colour and the wood beneath it

Coloured oil adds colour without covering the grain, so the wood can be seen through the colour. In a daycare centre, the colour can also help the children: for Vinge Daycare Centre we are making 92 children's cloakroom units in oiled pine plywood in red and blue, so the rows are divided up and the children quickly learn their own place.

At Mørkhøj School the wooden furniture is oiled in two colours, red on the lockers and blue on the tall cabinets and benches, so the surface can be maintained in patches for many years. We agreed the colours with the architect and the client before the furniture went into production.

Under the colour is pine plywood or birch plywood. Pine has a warm tone and a lively grain with knots. Birch is lighter and harder, and the layers are so thin that the edge shows as fine, straight stripes. The shoe racks for the sports hall are in birch plywood, and the columns and the long beam that runs through the hall are clad in the same board, so the furniture and the building belong together. What the choice means for a cabinet is explained under [plywood cabinets](/skabe-i-krydsfiner).

## Where plywood is not the right choice

Oiled plywood takes the moisture from wet jackets and wiping with a cloth, but not water that stands on it or soaks into the edge. In toilets and at wash counters we use [compact laminate](/kompaktlaminat), which is laminate all the way through and does not soak up water. At Vinge Daycare Centre the toilet cubicles are compact laminate, while the cloakrooms are plywood.

A cabinet in compact laminate costs almost twice as much as the same cabinet in pine plywood. That is why we use compact laminate where there is water, and plywood in the rest of the building. How plywood differs from the other boards used for furniture is explained in the guide [plywood, MDF or chipboard](/krydsfiner-mdf-eller-spaanplade).

## Requirements, documentation and drawings

Requirements for the surface and for certification are often in the general sections of the joinery specification and not under the individual item. We go through the whole specification and write the requirements down product by product before we price. If the tender requires FSC- or PEFC-certified wood, the quote states which boards can be supplied with certification. If the building is to carry the Nordic Swan Ecolabel, we choose boards that can be approved and collect the documentation for the material log. See [furniture for Nordic Swan Ecolabel buildings](/inventar-til-svanemaerket-byggeri).

The furniture is drawn in 3D, and the workshop drawings and the parts list come from the same model, so a changed dimension follows all the way through. For series of identical furniture, we are happy to build a sample piece first, so locks and hinges are tested before the rest is produced in our own production.

faq.q: Why do you use oil and not lacquer on plywood?
faq.a: The oil goes into the wood, so a worn corner or a scratch can be refreshed with new oil on site, without sanding down the whole piece of furniture. Lacquer gives a closed surface, but damage to the lacquer means the surface has to be sanded and lacquered again. If the joinery specification says lacquer, we price lacquer.

faq.q: Can plywood take water?
faq.a: Oiled plywood takes moisture from wet jackets and daily wiping, but not water that stands on the surface or soaks into the edge. In toilets and at wash counters we use compact laminate, which does not soak up water.

faq.q: Can the furniture have a different colour from the wood?
faq.a: Yes. Coloured oil adds colour while the grain can still be seen, and we agree the colour with the architect. If a door has to be one solid colour, it can get a high-pressure laminate face with the plywood edge visible around it.

faq.q: Can you supply FSC- or PEFC-certified plywood?
faq.a: If the tender requires it, the quote states which boards can be supplied with certification. If the building is to carry the Nordic Swan Ecolabel, we choose boards that can be approved and supply the documentation for the building's material log. The same documentation can be used in a DGNB building.

faq.q: How is oiled plywood maintained?
faq.a: Day to day with a well wrung-out cloth and a mild cleaning agent. When a spot is worn, it is lightly sanded and oiled with the same oil, and this can be done on site without taking the furniture down.

faq.q: What should we send to get a price?
faq.a: The drawings, the full joinery specification and the bill of quantities, and ideally the schedule with the installation date. Send it to tilbud@neminventar.dk, and you get a price per item, with reservations and questions gathered in the quote.

Oil, clear or coloured, and lacquer where the specification requires it
Wear is refreshed with oil on site
Compact laminate where water hits directly
Mørkhøj School, oiled in two colours
For FSC, PEFC and Nordic Swan Ecolabel buildings

h1: Shoe bench and storage bench made to measure
lead: A bench in oak veneer, 100 cm wide with two drawers under the seat and a cushion, costs DKK 8,450 incl. VAT flat-packed and collected. For the hallway, where the shoes go on. You build it in our 3D designer for benches and see the price as you choose.
body:
A bench in the hallway gives you a place to sit when your shoes go on, and a place to put them when you come home. Your bag can stand on the seat while you tie your laces, and the mittens can lie in a drawer under you.

You build the bench in [our 3D designer for benches](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=baenk). It can be 60 to 160 cm wide and 30 to 60 cm deep, and the seat is 42 cm above the floor. The price is on the screen as you choose, so you can try drawers and a shoe rack against each other.

## Shoe bench or bench with drawers

The first choice is what goes under the seat: an open shoe rack on two levels or up to three drawers side by side.

The shoe bench is open, so you put your shoes down without opening anything, and you can see which shoes are at home. Wet shoes dry in the air instead of in a closed drawer. The bench with a shoe rack has no plinth, so there is enough height for both levels, and it costs less than the bench with drawers, because there are no drawers to build.

With drawers, the bench becomes a storage bench that closes everything away, so the hallway looks tidy, even when there are many shoes. The drawers share the width of the bench, so three drawers in a 120 cm bench are about 40 cm wide each. They have a slot routed into the front to grip, or they open when you press them.

The prices are for benches in oak veneer with a cushion, incl. VAT and without delivery, and the bench is flat-packed.

| Bench in oak veneer with cushion | Under the seat | Price |
|---|---|---|
| 100 cm wide, 40 cm deep | 2 drawers | [DKK 8,450](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=baenk&t=e30) |
| 100 cm wide, 50 cm deep | 2 drawers | [DKK 9,200](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=baenk&t=eyJkIjo1MH0) |

| 160 cm wide, 40 cm deep | 3 drawers | [DKK 12,400](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=baenk&t=eyJiIjoxNjAsImJzayI6M30) |

## Bench with or without a cushion

The cushion is in grey upholstery fabric and lies on top of the seat. It makes the seat 48 cm high instead of 42 cm, and softer to sit on when the boots go on.

The cushion can be left out, and you will notice it in the price: on a bench in oak veneer, 100 cm wide with two drawers, the cushion adds DKK 2,850. Without a cushion, the seat is in the same material as the rest of the bench.

## The material

The bench is built in the same materials as our [wardrobes](/garderobeskab). Veneer is a thin layer of real wood on an MDF board, and it is oiled clear or in one of seven colours. Plywood is wood all the way through, in thin layers laid crosswise, and the layers show as stripes on the edges. Read more about [plywood](/skabe-i-krydsfiner).

The table shows the same bench, 100 cm wide and 40 cm deep, with two drawers and a cushion.

| Material | Price for the bench |
|---|---|
| Beech veneer | [DKK 8,375](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=baenk&t=eyJtYXQiOiJib2VnIn0) |
| Pine plywood | [DKK 8,250](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=baenk&t=eyJtYXQiOiJrcnlkcyJ9) |
| Oak veneer | [DKK 8,450](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=baenk&t=e30) |
| Birch plywood | [DKK 8,750](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=baenk&t=eyJtYXQiOiJiaXJrIn0) |

The four materials in the table are within DKK 500 of each other, so on the bench the choice under the seat matters more for the price than the material. Compact laminate is laminate all the way through and takes water and wear, and it can be worth considering in a hallway where wet boots come in.

## On its own or in a wall of cabinets

The bench can stand on its own, or it can sit in a wall of cabinets between the wardrobes. Then you build the whole wall in [the cabinet designer](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab), where one of the cabinets can be a bench with drawers and a cushion, and the bench gets the depth and material of the wall.

Above the bench there can be an [overhead cabinet](/overskabe) with doors at the top, level with the rest of the wall, or the space can be left open for jackets. If you add the frame, the overhead cabinet gets a cover panel on top and sides down to the floor, so the bench stands in an opening in the wall.

## From drawing to bench

When you send the bench from the designer, it is an enquiry, not an order. We send a quote and a drawing with the final measurements, and you approve the drawing before we build the bench in our own production. It takes 3 to 6 weeks from order to delivery, and we deliver throughout Denmark.

The bench is supplied flat-packed with assembly instructions, and the prices above are calculated that way. If you want it delivered assembled, there is an extra charge for freight, and if we are to carry it in and fix it to the wall, it must be assembled. You choose delivery for the whole order in the designer's basket, and the price is shown there before you send.

If the bench has to fit into a niche, write the measurements in the message. If the designer cannot do what you want, [send us a sketch](/kontakt?emne=B%C3%A6nk) with measurements.

faq.a: The shoe rack is chosen under the seat instead of drawers, and the price depends on width, depth and material. In [the designer](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=baenk) you see the price for your own measurements.

Build the whole wall in [the cabinet designer](https://designer.neminventar.dk/designer?p=hoejskab), where one of the cabinets can be a bench with drawers and a cushion, and an overhead cabinet can sit above the bench. A wall in oak veneer with two 60 cm wardrobes and a bench in between with two drawers, a cushion and an overhead cabinet costs DKK 33,600 incl. VAT and without delivery.

faq.a: The bench is supplied flat-packed with assembly instructions, and the prices are calculated that way. If you want it assembled, there is an extra charge for freight, and we can only carry the bench in and fix it to the wall if it is assembled. The price of delivery is shown in the designer's basket before you send.

h1: Workshop drawings and 3D model before production
lead: We draw all furniture in 3D before we produce it. The workshop drawings you approve and the parts list we build from come from the same model.
body:
Workshop drawings and the 3D model are what lies between the architect's drawing and the first cut in the board. The workshop drawings are what you approve before we go into production, and here you can read what they show and what to look for.

## The architect's drawing is not a workshop drawing

The architect's drawing shows what the furniture should look like, and the workshop drawing shows how it will be built. An architect's drawing of a cloakroom shows dimensions and layout, but rarely how the sides are joined or how the furniture is fixed to the wall. Those are decisions we make when we draw up the furniture in 3D, and they become visible on the workshop drawings.

We model each part separately, so the model knows which board the part is cut from. The workshop drawings show each piece of furniture from the front and from above with dimensions and, where needed, a section or an enlarged joint. In plywood, where the layers show at the edge, this is where you can see which edges are left visible and how the corners meet.

## One model for drawing and parts list

The parts list comes from the same model, with every part, its material and its dimensions. That is what production cuts from. Because the drawing and the parts list come from the same place, they cannot get out of step with each other. If a dimension changes after approval, we correct the model, and the new drawing and the new parts list come out of it together, so nobody builds from an old drawing.

## What to look for when you approve

You know the dimensions and layout from your own drawings. What is new on the workshop drawing is what the architect's drawing did not show, e.g. which edges are left visible and how the furniture is fixed.

The fixing is worth looking at early. A shelving unit or a bench hung on a lightweight wall needs something to fix into, and the reinforcement in the wall has to be in place before the wall is closed. When the workshop drawings show where the furniture is to be fixed, whoever builds the wall has time to put the reinforcement in the right place.

The same goes for the other trades. A power socket in a [seating niche](/siddenicher-og-baenke) or water and drainage for a [kitchenette](/tekoekkener-og-koekkenoer) has to have its place in the furniture before we produce, so the electrician and the plumber know where to end up.

## Measured on site and tested in one sample

Where a dimension depends on the building, we measure on site before we produce. A [wall-to-wall shelving unit](/reoler-paa-maal) has to fit the wall as it was built, and that can differ from the drawing.

For series with many identical elements, we prefer to build a sample piece first. A fault in a joint or a lock costs one piece of furniture when it is found in the sample piece, and the whole series when it is found too late. The sample piece also shows the real board with the real oil, which a colour sample on paper cannot, because the oil takes differently on pine and birch.

For Mørkhøj School each room is drawn in 3D and approved before it goes into production, and colours and materials have been agreed with the architect and the client. The wooden furniture is oiled in two colours mixed for the project.

The model also shows how the modules are joined into one piece of furniture and fixed to the wall, so the installation is planned before we arrive on site. If you are an architect, you can read more about how we work from [your drawings and specification](/inventar-til-arkitekter), and if you want a price, see [what to include in your enquiry](/forespoergsel-paa-fast-inventar).

faq.q: Do you supply workshop drawings for approval?

h1: Shoe racks and shoe shelves for schools and sports halls
lead: A shoe rack gets water and grit carried in every day. We build it in oiled plywood that can be repaired on site, and it can have a grille in the bottom and a bench to sit on.
body:
Shoe racks in schools and sports halls stand where the outdoors comes inside. Water and grit from the schoolyard come with the shoes onto the shelf, and the shelf is swept and washed every day. That is what we build the shoe racks for.

## The grit wears more than the shoes

It is the grit under the shoes that wears a shoe rack. It stays on the shelf and is pushed back and forth every time a shoe is put down and picked up again, and it works like sandpaper on the surface.

That is why, as a starting point, we oil the shoe racks instead of lacquering them. Once a lacquer film is scratched through, water gets into the wood at that spot, and the damage can rarely be repaired locally without it showing. The oil sits in the wood, so a worn shelf can be re-oiled on site without sanding down the whole unit.

The bottom can have a grille, so grit and water fall through and do not stay under the shoes. In the children's cloakroom units we are making for Vinge Daycare Centre, each module has a deeper bottom with a shoe grille for shoes and boots. See [furniture for daycare centres](/inventar-til-daginstitutioner).

## Wet footwear has to be able to dry

An open shoe rack lets the shoes dry in the air. In a closed cabinet the moisture stays put, and then it starts to smell. If the shoes have to stand behind a door, the door can have holes, so air can get through even when it is closed.

Where there is water all day, as near the showers in a changing room or a swimming pool, the shelves can be made of [compact laminate](/kompaktlaminat). The board does not soak up water, not even at the edges, where wood would swell. The shoe rack can also stand on legs, so the floor underneath can be washed.

## Shoes come off sitting down

Anyone taking boots off or putting them on would rather sit down. That is why we often build the shoe rack and the seat together.

For a sports hall we have made 43 shoe racks in birch plywood in a long row along the corridor with a bench on top, so you can sit down and look from the corridor into the hall. The columns and the beam above the row are clad in the same plywood, so the furniture and the building belong together. See [furniture for sports halls](/inventar-til-idraetshaller).

At Mørkhøj School we are delivering 342 lockers with a bench and shoe racks for the pupils, so shoes and outdoor clothes are kept in one place. For Hou School we are building open shoe racks in pine plywood with a seat, so low that they are both storage and a bench. See also [lockers](/lockers) and [cloakrooms](/garderober).

## The shelf spacing follows the users

Children's shoes in a daycare centre and rubber boots in a school cloakroom do not need the same distance between the shelves. We draw the spacing and the number of places for the people who will use the shoe rack, and for how many will take their shoes off at the same time.

The surface can be clear oil or coloured oil in the same colour as the rest of the cloakroom. We draw the shoe racks in 3D to the room's dimensions, and you approve the drawings before we make them in our own production.

faq.q: What do you do about wet shoes and grit?
faq.a: The bottom can have a grille, so water and grit fall through and can be swept up from the floor. Where there is water all day, as near the showers, the shelves can be made of compact laminate, which does not soak up water.

faq.q: Why oil and not lacquer on the shoe racks?
faq.a: The grit scratches the surface. Once the lacquer is scratched through, water gets into the wood, and the damage can rarely be repaired locally without it showing. An oiled shelf can be re-oiled on site.

faq.q: Can the shoe rack be combined with a bench?
faq.a: Yes. The bench can sit on top of the shoe rack and run the full length of the row, as on the 43 shoe racks we have made for a sports hall, or the seat can be built into a low shoe shelf.

faq.q: Can shoe racks sit under lockers?
faq.a: Yes. The shoe rack can sit under the lockers with a bench in front, so each pupil has shoes and outdoor clothes in one place.

faq.q: Can the shoe racks be made in colours?
faq.a: Yes. Coloured oil lets the grain of the wood show through, and the colour can follow the rest of the cloakroom. The colour is agreed with the architect.
